text: Do not make data members const or references in a copyable/movable type.
Avoid trivial getters and setters (an accessor that only returns/assigns a member).
If you define or delete any copy/move/destructor, define or delete them all (rule of five).
A base class destructor should be public+virtual or protected+non-virtual.
A member function that uses no instance state should be static or free (make a function a member only if it needs the object).
By default, declare single-argument constructors explicit.
Initialize all data members.
Minimize exposure of members (avoid needless public data).
Prefer the standard library to hand-crafted code (use std algorithms over raw loops).
Always initialize an object/variable.
Do not use macros for constants or functions; prefer constexpr/inline.
Keep pointer use simple; avoid pointer arithmetic.
Avoid "magic" constants; use symbolic/named constants.
Avoid lossy/implicit arithmetic conversions.
Avoid casts; especially reinterpret_cast and C-style casts.
Prefer a range-for to a plain index for-loop where possible.
Avoid do-while loops.
Do not rely on implicit fallthrough in switch statements.
For "in" parameters, pass cheaply-copied types by value and others by reference to const; avoid unnecessary by-value copies.
A function should perform a single logical operation.
To return multiple values, prefer a struct/tuple over many out-parameters.
Keep the number of function arguments low.
Avoid calling new and delete explicitly.
Use unique_ptr or shared_ptr to represent ownership.
A raw pointer (T*) is non-owning; do not own a resource through a raw pointer.
Prefer std::array or std::vector to C-style arrays.
Avoid reinterpret_cast; do not use unsafe casts.
